title: Impact of Co-mutations and Transcriptional Signatures in Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients Treated with Adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 Trial
author: Marcelo V Negrao; Alvaro G Paula; David Molkentine; Laura Hover; Monique Nilsson; Natalie Vokes; Lars Engstrom; Andrew Calinisan; David M Briere; Laura Waters; Jill Hallin; Lixia Diao; Mehmet Altan; George R Blumenschein; Ferdinandos Skoulidis; Jing Wang; Scott E Kopetz; David S Hong; Don L Gibbons; Peter Olson; James G Christensen; John V Heymach
text:
Abstract
Purpose:
KRAS inhibitors are revolutionizing the treatment of non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but clinico-genomic determinants of treatment efficacy warrant continued exploration.
Experimental Design:
Patients with advanced KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC treated with adagrasib [KRYSTAL-1 (NCT03785249)] were included in the analysis. Pretreatment next-generation sequencing data were collected per protocol. HTG EdgeSeq Transcriptome Panel was used for gene expression profiling. Clinical endpoints included objective response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC cell lines and xenograft models were used for sensitivity analyses and combination drug screens.
Results:
KEAP1 MUT and STK11MUT were associated with shorter survival to adagrasib [KEAP1: PFS 4.1 vs. 9.9 months, HR 2.7, P < 0.01; OS 5.4 vs. 19.0 months, HR 3.6, P < 0.01; STK11: PFS 4.2 vs. 11.0 months, HR 2.2, P < 0.01; OS 9.8 months vs. not reached (NR), HR 2.6, P < 0.01]. KEAP1WT/STK11WT status identified adagrasib-treated patients with significantly longer PFS (16.9 months) and OS (NR). Preclinical analyses further validate the association between KEAP1 loss of function and adagrasib resistance. Adagrasib and mTOR inhibitor combinations produced higher treatment efficacy in NSCLC models harboring STK11 and KEAP1 co-mutations. NRF2HIGH signaling was associated with shorter survival to adagrasib (PFS: 4.2 vs. 8.4 months, HR 2.0, P = 0.02; OS: 6.5 vs. 19.0 months, HR 2.8, P < 0.01) even in patients with KEAP1WT NSCLC. KEAP1WT/STK11WT/NRF2LOW status identified patients—32%—with longer survival to adagrasib (PFS 12.0 vs. 4.2 months, HR 0.2, P < 0.01; OS NR vs. 8.0 months, HR 0.1, P < 0.01).
Conclusions:
KEAP1, STK11, and NRF2 status define patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC with markedly distinct outcomes to adagrasib. These results further support the use of genomic features—mutational and nonmutational—for the treatment selection of patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC.
Translational Relevance.
KRAS G12C inhibitors are revolutionizing the treatment of solid tumors, particularly non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but individual patients experience heterogeneous clinical outcomes ranging from early progression to durable clinical benefit. In this work, we demonstrate that tumor genomic features such as KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutations and NRF2 signaling are each associated with shorter survival to adagrasib monotherapy in patients treated in the KRYSTAL-1 trial. Collectively, these tumor genomic characteristics define a subgroup of patients—32% of the study cohort—with significant and meaningfully longer survival to adagrasib monotherapy. In addition, we demonstrate that adagrasib and mTOR inhibitor combinations increase treatment efficacy in KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC harboring KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutations. Our results further demonstrate the impact of genomic features—mutational and nonmutational—on clinical outcomes of KRAS G12C inhibitors and support the clinical development of novel combinations for the treatment of KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC.
Introduction
KRAS mutations are present in approximately 30% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC), and of these, approximately 42% are G12C mutations (1). Although formerly considered undruggable, the development of covalent allosteric off-state allele-specific KRAS G12C inhibitors (KRAS G12Ci) has enabled successful targeting of KRAS. In the phase II registration enabling cohorts of the CodeBreak 100 and KRYSTAL-1 trials, sotorasib and adagrasib produced objective response rates (ORR) of 37% and 43%, respectively (2, 3). This led the FDA to grant accelerated approval for both compounds in 2021 and 2022, respectively. However, progression-free survival (PFS) with these agents is approximately 7 months (2, 3), which is inferior to other small molecule inhibitors approved for the treatment of oncogene-addicted NSCLC (e.g., EGFR, ALK, and ROS1; refs. 4–6). In the phase III CodeBreak 200 trial, sotorasib only modestly improved PFS compared with docetaxel monotherapy in patients with previously treated KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC (5.6 vs. 4.5 months, HR 0.66, P = 0.0017), and there was no difference in overall survival (OS) between the groups (10.6 vs. 11.3 months, HR 1.0, P = 0.53; ref. 7). Head-to-head comparison of adagrasib and docetaxel in patients with previously treated advanced KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC in the phase III KRYSTAL-12 trial showed similar results (8).
In the largest cohort to date of patients with advanced KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC treated with sotorasib and adagrasib (N = 424 pts), we demonstrated that KEAP1 (KEAP1MUT) and STK11 co-mutations (STK11MUT) are enriched in early disease progression to KRAS G12Ci (9). KEAP1MUT were also independently associated with shorter PFS and OS to sotorasib and adagrasib. Despite being enriched for early disease progression, STK11MUT were not independently associated with PFS and OS in a deconvolution analysis that accounted for KEAP1 co-mutation status (9). Similar results were observed in another retrospective cohort of patients treated with KRAS G12Ci (10). One of the main effects of KEAP1 loss of function is increased NRF2 activation, which promotes increased cellular fitness and detoxification (11, 12). Although increased NRF2 signaling has been associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) resistance (13), its clinical impact on KRAS G12Ci efficacy remains unknown. Collectively, these findings highlight a continued need to further evaluate determinants of clinical outcomes to KRAS G12Ci to improve treatment selection and facilitate drug discovery. To address this unmet need, we interrogated clinico-genomic data from a cohort of patients with advanced KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC treated with adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 trial (NCT03785249). Additionally, KRASG12C NSCLC cell lines and xenograft models were used to interrogate biomarkers of clinical benefit, or lack thereof, to adagrasib and to determine rational combinations to improve treatment efficacy.
Materials and Methods
Study population—KRYSTAL-1 trial
The KRYSTAL-1 cohort consisted of patients with previously treated advanced KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC who received single-agent adagrasib 600 mg orally twice daily on expansion cohorts 1B and A of the trial (NCT03785249)—N = 129 patients. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the U.S. Common Rule. All patients signed informed consent for trial enrollment. All necessary approvals were obtained from the relevant ethics committees and institutional review boards. Patient demographic information (e.g., age, sex) was collected as part of the trial.
Tumor profiling
There were 121 patients with next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed in pre-adagrasib treatment samples (NGS evaluable patients). Eight patients did not have NGS results available and were excluded from the co-mutation analyses. NGS results were available from participating institutions’ preapproved local assays, and NGS data were collected as part of the clinical data for the KRYSTAL-1 trial. All 121 patients had tumor tissue NGS results, and 71 had both tumor tissue and blood NGS results. Qualifying deleterious variants for tumor suppressor genes were defined as follows: (i) homozygous deletions, (ii) nonsense mutations, (iii) frameshift deletion/insertion mutations, and (iv) nonsynonymous single nucleotide mutations and/or splice-site mutations that were reported in the COSMIC database (RRID:SCR_002260) with N > 5 and mutation assessor structural impact scores noted as likely exhibiting a functional/structural impact and/or the mutated codon and corresponding amino acid were identified as a statistically significant recurrent hotspot in population-scale cohorts of tumor samples from various cancer types (3, 14). Patients were allocated to co-mutation groups based on the presence or absence of a deleterious variant for a given gene. The denominator for a co-mutation rate is the number of patients with NGS results available from a panel with coverage for a given tumor suppressor gene. The numerator for a co-mutation rate is the number of patients with a qualifying deleterious variant detected in an NGS panel with coverage for a given tumor suppressor gene.
Gene expression profiling was performed in pre-adagrasib treatment tissue samples from 68 patients that had available tissue—gene expression evaluable population—using the HTG EdgeSeq Transcriptome Panel at HTG Molecular per the manufacturer’s instructions. The sequencing data have been deposited in the NCBI database (BioProject-PRJNA591860) and as Supplementary Material as previously reported (15). The data are publicly available at the date of publication. Raw counts were normalized by library size, and log2 counts per million (CPM) expression values were calculated for each sample (edgeR v3.32.1; RRID:SCR_012802). Signature scores were calculated as mean log2 CPM values for all signature genes with mean log2 CPM ≥1. NRF2 signaling was assessed by NRF2 score (13) and included the 38 genes that were covered in the transcriptome panel and that had mean log2 CPM ≥1. A similar approach was used for STK11/LKB1 (13/16 covered genes; ref. 16) and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) signatures (76/77 covered genes). The mesenchymal phenotype was defined as mesenchymal–epithelial markers score >0 (17).
Statistical analyses
The Kaplan–Meier method was used to estimate PFS and OS, and differences were assessed by log-rank test. HR and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using the Cox proportional hazards model. Objective response was determined through RECIST version 1.1 (18). Differences in categorical variables were assessed by a two-sided chi-square test. Significance was established at P ≤ 0.05. Statistical analysis was performed in R (version 4.0.2; RRID:SCR_001905) using the survival package (version 3.1-12; RRID:SCR_021137) and visualized using Survminer (version 0.4.9; RRID:SCR_021094).
Cell culture
Cell lines were purchased from ATCC and maintained at 37°C and 5% CO2 in RPMI 1640 medium (Corning, 10-040-CV) supplemented with heat-inactivated 10% FBS (Sigma), 1% L-glutamine (Corning), and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Corning). Cell lines were thawed from stock vials at passages 3 to 6 and kept in culture for no longer than 3 months.
Cell lines were validated by short tandem repeat (STR) DNA fingerprinting using the Promega 16 High Sensitivity STR Kit (catalog # DC2100). The STR profiles were compared with online search databases (DSMZ/ATCC/JCRB/RIKEN) of approximately 2,500 known profiles, along with the MD Anderson Characterized Cell Line Core database of approximately 2,600 known profiles. The STR profiles matched known DNA fingerprints or were unique. STR DNA fingerprinting was done by the Cytogenetics and Cell Authentication Core at MD Anderson Cancer Center.
Cell lines were confirmed clean of mycoplasma contamination by detection with MycoAlert Mycoplasma Detection Kit (Lonza, LT07-418) following manufacturer’s guidelines for ratio interpretation: <0.9, negative for mycoplasma; 0.9 to 1.2, borderline: quarantine cells and retest in 24 hours; and >1.2, mycoplasma contamination.
Cell viability assay
Cell viability was measured using CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega, G7573). A total of 5,000 cells/100 µL per well were seeded in a 96-well Nunclon delta white microwell plate (Thermo Fisher, 136101) and incubated overnight until cells were attached. The next day, increasing doses of adagrasib were diluted in media and added to the dish containing cells. Cells were incubated in adagrasib for 7 days, and then 40 µL of CellTiter-Glo was added per well and incubated for 5 minutes covered and shaking. Luminescence was read using a FLUOstar OPTIMA microplate reader (BMG Labtech), and data were normalized to DMSO control. Combination viability experiments were seeded as above. Then, the cells were treated for 5 days with an increasing concentration gradient of adagrasib and everolimus or the combination, or adagrasib and trametinib or the combination. CellTiter-Glo (40 µL) was added per well and incubated for 5 minutes covered and shaking. Luminescence was read using a FLUOstar OPTIMA microplate reader (BMG Labtech), and data were normalized to DMSO control. Bliss synergy scores and 3D contour maps were generated using SynergyFinder+ (RRID:SCR_019318).
Colony formation assay
Clonogenicity was tested following treatment with adagrasib, mTOR inhibitors AZD8055 and everolimus, and MEK inhibitors selumetinib and trametinib or the combination of adagrasib and mTORi or adagrasib and MEK inhibitors. Briefly, adherent cells were detached by trypsinization and counted using a Countess II Automated Cell Counter (Invitrogen) and normalized to 1 cell/μL in media; 250 and 500 single cells per well were plated for H2030 (RRID:CVCL_1517), and 500 and 1,000 single cells per well were plated for H23 (RRID:CVCL_1547). Each cell number was plated in triplicate in a six-well dish and incubated overnight until cells were attached. The next day, each individual agent or the combinations were diluted in media and added to the dishes containing cells. The agents were left on for the entirety of the assay until visible colonies were formed (12 days). All colonies containing greater than 50 cells were manually counted, and all data were normalized to DMSO control. Graphs were generated using GraphPad Prism 10.0.3 (RRID:SCR_002798), and P values were calculated by one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons.
Please refer to Supplementary Methods S1 for additional information on in vitro experiments.
In vivo tumor growth inhibition in CDX and PDX models
All mouse studies were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and were conducted in compliance with all applicable regulations and guidelines from the NIH. Mice were maintained under pathogen-free conditions, and food and water were provided ad libitum. Four-to-eight-week-old, female, immune-compromised mice were inoculated by subcutaneous injection with a human cell line–derived tumor cells, patient-derived tumor cells, or patient-derived xenograft (PDX) fragments in the right hind flank. Mouse health was monitored daily, and caliper measurements began when tumors were palpable. Tumor volume measurements were determined utilizing the formula 0.5 × L × W2 in which L refers to the length and W refers to the width of each tumor. When tumors reached an average tumor volume of ∼250 to 400 mm3, mice were randomized into treatment groups. Mice were treated once daily by oral gavage with either vehicle consisting of 10% Captisol (CyDex Pharmaceuticals) in 50-mmol/L citrate buffer pH 5.0 or adagrasib formulated in vehicle at 100 mg/kg. Animals were monitored daily, and body weight and tumors were measured 2 to 3 times per week. The cell line–derived xenograft (CDX) models CALU1 (RRID:CVCL_0608), HCC44 (RRID:CVCL_2060), LU65 (RRID:CVCL_1392), LU99 (RRID:CVCL_3015), NCI-H1373 (RRID:CVCL_1465), NCI-H2030 (RRID:CVCL_1517), NCI-H2122 (RRID:CVCL_1531), NCI-H358 (RRID:CVCL_1559), and SW1573 (RRID:CVCL_1720) were conducted by Mirati Therapeutics. The PDX models LU11693, LU1147, LU11554, LU11692, LU2512, LU2529, LU5191, LU5212, LU5245, and LU6405 were sponsored by Mirati Therapeutics and conducted by Crown Bioscience. The PDX models ST1328, ST1506, ST1545, ST171, ST1989, ST2972, ST396, ST4134B, ST4341, and STF005 were sponsored by Mirati Therapeutics and conducted by XenoSTART. Statistical analysis of the in vivo efficacy of adagrasib in NSCLC KRAS G12C models based on KEAP1 and STK11 genotypes was performed using a one-sided, unpaired, nonparametric Mann–Whitney test in GraphPad Prism (RRID:SCR_002798). Significance was established at P ≤ 0.05.
In vivo adagrasib anchored CRISPR screen
A custom single-guide RNA (sgRNA) lentiviral library was generated at Cellecta comprising five sgRNAs targeting ∼1,000 genes including ∼10 positive and negative controls. Positive controls consisted of sgRNAs targeting essential genes, whereas negative controls consisted of sgRNAs targeting introns of various genes. Parental cells were first transduced with a Cas9 lentiviral construct and selected with blasticidin. After determining the functional titer of the concentrated lentiviral sgRNA library lentiviral stock, the stable Cas9-expressing cell pools were transduced with the sgRNA lentiviral library and selected with puromycin for 3 to 5 days. Cells were transduced such that at least 500 cells per sgRNA construct were transduced with each sgRNA construct (∼5,000), for each replicate (5 × 106 transduced cells/replicate). The multiplicity of infection was ∼0.3 to ensure the majority of transduced cells were transduced with only one lentivirus (∼8 × 106 cells plated for transduction/replicate). After puromycin selection, cells were further expanded to enable implantation of 5 × 106cells/mouse 1:1 of Matrigel and PBS into 20 to 25 immunocompromised mice as well as collection of a baseline sample (5 × 106 cells). Tumors were grown until they reached a volume of ∼125 to 175 mm3, and five xenografts were harvested for in vivo day 0. Five tumor-bearing animals were then dosed with either vehicle or adagrasib at 100 mg/kg orally every day for 2 weeks, and whole tumors were harvested. Baseline and tumor samples were sent to Cellecta for DNA isolation, sgRNA amplification by PCR, and NGS. Replicates exhibited good agreement as did the different sgRNAs targeting the same gene, and both positive and negative controls behaved as expected. The sgRNA raw counts were log2 transformed and normalized using the relative log expression method (edgeR version 3.22.3—SCR_012802). All samples cluster according to treatment and cell lines in the principal component analysis, and no batch effects were found. Relative log2 fold change (FC) in sgRNA abundance of samples versus sgRNA representation in the plasmid NGS quality control dataset were calculated using the median log2 CPM values in R (version 3.6.1; RRID:SCR_001905). The differential expression of sgRNAs was identified by contrasting drug-treated samples versus vehicle-treated samples. Log2 FC at the gene level was calculated using the average median log2 CPM values and plotted using customized R scripts. Differences between adagrasib- and vehicle-treated samples were assessed with a two-tailed t test and adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedures. Significance was established at P ≤ 0.05 and adjusted at P ≤ 0.20. Adagrasib CRISPR screen data are available in Supplementary Table S1.
CRISPR-engineered LU99 models
Parental LU99 cells (RCB1900, RIKEN BRC; RRID:CVCL_3015) were stably transduced with Cas9 lentivirus (pRCCB-CMV-Cas9-2A-Blast, SVC9B-PS; Cellecta) and selected with blasticidin. The LU99 Cas9-expressing cell pool was subsequently transduced with lentivirus from pRSG16-U6-sg-UbiC-TagRFP-2A-Puro (CVCRC-PX 93658-3P, Cellecta) containing an sgRNA guide (5′-CAGCACCGTTCATGACGTGG-3′) targeting KEAP1 (reference sequence: NM_203500.1), selected with puromycin and expanded to isolate single-cell clones. The KEAP1 genotype of single-cell clones was determined by Sanger sequencing and interleukin-1β converting enzyme analysis (19) against a LU99 parental control. The KEAP1 knockout (KO) clones 1 and 2 were selected with an interleukin-1β converting enzyme percent INDEL of 94% and 83%, respectively. In parallel, an LU99 nontargeting sgRNA transduced model was also established as a pool (sgRNA target sequence 5′-CAGCACCGTTCATGACGTGG-3′) following transduction of the LU99 Cas9 cells and puromycin selection.
LU99 KEAP1 KO in vivo tumor growth inhibition study
The LU99 nontargeting sgRNA and LU99 KEAP1 KO models were used to perform an in vivo tumor growth inhibition study. For each LU99 model, 6-to-8-week-old, female, athymic nude-Foxn1nu mice (Envigo; RRID:IMSR_ENV:HSD-069) were injected subcutaneously with tumor cells in 100 μL of PBS and Matrigel matrix in the right hind flank with 5 × 106 cells (Corning #356237; Discovery Labware) 1:1 cells:Matrigel. Mouse health was monitored daily, and caliper measurements began when tumors were palpable. Tumor volume measurements were determined utilizing the formula 0.5 × L × W2 in which L refers to the length and W refers to the width of each tumor. When tumors reached an average tumor volume of ∼350 to 400 mm3, mice were randomized into treatment groups. Mice were treated by oral gavage with either vehicle consisting of 10% research grade Captisol (CyDex Pharmaceuticals) in 50-mmol/L citrate buffer pH 5.0 or adagrasib in the vehicle at indicated doses. For efficacy studies, animals were orally administered adagrasib or vehicle and monitored daily, tumors were measured three times per week, and body weights were measured two times per week. Statistical analysis of the engineered LU99 in vivo models was performed comparing the adagrasib-treated groups (LU99 nontargeting sgRNA transduced model vs. sgKEAP1 KO clones) using a two-sided unpaired t test in GraphPad Prism (RRID:SCR_002798). Significance was established at P-value ≤0.05.
Data availability
Clinical trial data may be shared with qualified researchers, upon request, following the criteria, timelines, and process detailed at https://www.bms.com/researchers-and-partners/independent-research/data-sharing-request-process.html. RNA sequencing data have been deposited at the NCBI database (BioProject-PRJNA591860) and are available as Supplementary Material as previously reported (15).
Results
KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutations are associated with worse clinical outcomes with adagrasib treatment
A total of 121 patients were included in the co-mutation analyses. The data cutoff for cohorts 1B and A is October 15, 2021. Median age was 64 years (range: 25–89), 57% of patients were female, and 96% were current or former smokers; 18% and 82% of patients had Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status scores of 0 and 1, respectively. The median number of prior lines of systemic therapies was two (Supplementary Table S2). The most frequently co-mutated genes in the study population were STK11 (47%; 47/100), TP53 (39%; 41/106), KEAP1 (30%; 27/91), ATM (25%; 22/89), and CDKN2A (22%; 15/67).
Patients whose tumor harbored KEAP1MUT or STK11MUT had significantly worse PFS and OS upon treatment with adagrasib [KEAP1: PFS 4.1 vs. 9.9 months, HR 2.7 (95% CI, 1.6–4.7), log-rank P < 0.01; OS 5.4 vs. 19.0 months, HR 3.6 (95% CI, 2.0–6.6), log-rank P < 0.01; STK11: PFS 4.2 vs. 11.0 months, HR 2.2 (95% CI, 1.3–3.6), log-rank P < 0.01; OS 9.8 months vs. not reached (NR), HR 2.6, (95% CI, 1.4–4.7), log-rank P < 0.01; Fig. 1A–D]. Patients whose tumor harbored a KEAP1MUT showed numerically lower ORR (30% vs. 53%, chi-square P = 0.07), and there was no difference in ORR according to STK11 co-mutation status (45% vs. 45%, chi-square P = 1.00; Fig. 1E and F). Because STK11MUT and KEAP1MUT frequently co-occur in NSCLC, we performed a deconvolution analysis to further evaluate the impact of each gene. Patients whose tumor was KEAP1WT/STK11WT had significant and meaningfully longer PFS (16.9 months) and OS (NR) compared with patients whose tumor was KEAP1MUT and/or STK11MUT (Fig. 2A and B). Patients whose tumor harbored a KEAP1MUT had numerically lower ORR (Fig. 2C). TP53, ATM, and CDKN2A co-mutations were not associated with clinical outcomes upon treatment with adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 trial (Supplementary Fig. S1A–S1I).
KEAP1 co-mutations are associated with resistance to adagrasib in lung cancer preclinical models
To further evaluate the efficacy of adagrasib according to co-mutation status of KEAP1 and STK11, we leveraged four different KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC cell lines with differential sensitivity to adagrasib: H358, KEAP1WT/STK11WT were categorized as sensitive; H23 and H2030, KEAP1MUT/STK11MUT as partially sensitive; and HCC44, KEAP1MUT/STK11MUT as resistant to adagrasib (Supplementary Fig. S2A). We noted that intracellular concentrations of on-state KRAS-GTP differ upon treatment with adagrasib across the four cell lines. Adagrasib produced continuous suppression of KRAS-GTP between 6 and 48 hours in H358 cells compared with control. Meanwhile, adagrasib treatment produced an initial decrease of KRAS-GTP at 6 hours followed by an increase at 24 and 48 hours when compared with control in the partially sensitive cell lines H23 and H2030. The resistant cell line HCC44 showed persistently elevated KRAS-GTP concentration upon treatment with adagrasib (Supplementary Fig. S2B). Using a lentiviral vector, we then expressed wild-type KEAP1 or STK11/LKB1 in the KEAP1MUT/STK11MUT H23, H2030, and HCC44 cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S2C). KEAP1 reexpression led to a significant increase in sensitivity to adagrasib in all three cell lines in 7-day cell viability assays (Fig. 3A–C). Expression of STK11/LKB1 also increased sensitivity to adagrasib in H2030 and HCC44 cell lines, but not in the H23 cell line (Fig. 3A–C), which suggests that KEAP1 loss of function may exert a more dominant effect in this model.
We also evaluated the effect of KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutations on the efficacy of adagrasib monotherapy in in vivo KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC models using a broad panel of CDX and PDX. KEAP1MUT/STK11MUT (red) and KEAP1MUT/STK11WT (blue) models had lower response rates—33% and 60%, respectively—compared with KEAP1WT models [STK11WT (gray): 71% and STK11MUT (purple): 75%; Fig. 3D]. Furthermore, KEAP1MUT/STK11MUT models had the lowest median percentage tumor regression upon treatment with adagrasib (Fig. 3D).
Next, we performed in vivo CRISPR/Cas9 KO screens of over 900 genes using the adagrasib sensitive KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC LU99 model (KEAP1WT/STK11WT) to interrogate candidate genes that may modulate response to adagrasib. sgRNAs targeting KEAP1 were the most significantly enriched for resistance in adagrasib-treated models across all screened genes (log2 FC 3.1, P = 0.01; Fig. 3E). KEAP1 loss has also been previously reported to promote increased cellular fitness in the H2122 KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC model and in KRASG12D-mutant models treated with adagrasib or MRTX1133—a KRAS G12D inhibitor—respectively (20, 21). Interestingly, sgRNAs targeting STK11 were not enriched for resistance to adagrasib in this model. sgRNAs targeting tumor suppressor genes PTEN, TSC1, and RB1 were enriched for resistance to adagrasib, while sgRNAs targeting CDK4 and PRMT5 were enriched for increased sensitivity to adagrasib (Fig. 3E).
We then generated xenograft models using the LU99 CRISPR KO clones to further assess the impact of KEAP1 loss of function in vivo. Both nontargeting and KEAP1 targeting models treated with adagrasib had significant reduction in tumor volume compared with vehicle control. However, the KEAP1 KO models began to have tumor regrowth starting on day 20 and had significant growth on day 30 despite continued adagrasib treatment (Fig. 3F), which is suggestive of the early emergence of adaptive resistance.
Adagrasib and mTOR inhibitor combinations promote increased antitumor activity in KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC harboring co-mutations associated with resistance to KRAS G12Ci
Next, we sought to identify combinations that would be effective for the treatment of KEAP1MUT and STK11MUTKRASG12C-mutant NSCLC. We performed broad drug screens using KRASG12C-mutant lung cancer cell lines to identify combinations with higher efficacy compared with adagrasib monotherapy. Adagrasib combinations with mTOR or MEK inhibitors showed increased efficacy in H23 and HCC44 cell lines (partially sensitive and resistant to adagrasib, respectively; Fig. 4A; Supplementary Fig. S3A). We further investigated the efficacy of these combinations in the H23 and H2030 models. Adagrasib combinations with ATP-competitive mTORC1/2 inhibitor AZD8055 and rapamycin analog everolimus both showed significant reduction in surviving cell fraction compared with either single-agent alone and relative to control in 12-day clonogenicity assays (Fig. 4B). We observed marked inhibition of S6 phosphorylation (Ser235/236) with everolimus and the adagrasib and everolimus combination, but not with adagrasib alone, across both partially sensitive and resistant cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S3B). Adagrasib combinations with MEK inhibitors selumetinib and trametinib also reduced surviving cell fraction compared with either agent alone and relative to control in 12-day clonogenicity assays (Fig. 4C). However, the adagrasib and selumetinib combination did not inhibit S6 phosphorylation in either adagrasib partially sensitive and resistant cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S3B).
NRF2 signaling is associated with worse clinical outcomes upon treatment with adagrasib
KEAP1 functions as a tumor suppressor gene by regulating NRF2 intracellular concentration through ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (11, 22–24). NRF2 is a master regulator of cellular oxidative stress (11, 12). When expressed, NRF2 binds to an antioxidant response element enhancer and promotes the transcription of key genes associated with cellular detoxification and enhanced cellular fitness (12). Since KEAP1MUT was associated with shorter PFS and OS to adagrasib monotherapy (Fig. 1), we hypothesized that increased NRF2 activation would also be associated with worse clinical outcomes to adagrasib. Baseline tumor samples from 68 patients treated with adagrasib on the KRYSTAL-1 trial underwent transcriptomic profiling, and these patients were included in this analysis. Clinical characteristics of the gene expression evaluable patients were similar to the overall KRYSTAL-1 cohort and to the NGS evaluable patients (Supplementary Table S2). NRF2 transcriptional score was used as a surrogate for NRF2 signaling (see “Materials and Methods”; ref. 13). As expected, NRF2HIGH score was enriched in KEAP1MUT tumors relative to KEAP1WT (Supplementary Fig. S4A and S4B). NRF2HIGH score was negatively correlated with PFS (R −0.30; P = 0.01) and OS (R −0.25; P = 0.04) upon treatment with adagrasib (Fig. 5A and B). There was no difference in ORR to adagrasib according to the NRF2 score (Supplementary Fig. S4C). When using median as the cutoff to define NRF2HIGH status, patients with NRF2HIGH tumors had shorter PFS and OS compared with those with NRF2LOW tumors [PFS 4.2 vs. 8.4 months, HR 2.0 (95% CI, 1.1–3.6), log-rank P = 0.02; OS 6.5 vs. 19.0 months, HR 2.8 (95% CI, 1.3–5.7), log-rank P < 0.01; Fig. 5C and D]. Similar results were observed when using upper tertile and upper quartile as the definition for NRF2HIGH status (Supplementary Fig. S5A–S5D). NRF2HIGH score was also negatively correlated with PFS to adagrasib monotherapy in patients whose tumor was KEAP1WT (N = 35, R −0.39, P = 0.02; Fig. 5E), STK11WT (N = 23, R −0.46, P = 0.03), and KEAP1WT/STK11WT (N = 18, R −0.36, P = 0.15; Supplementary Fig. S6A and S6B). Similar results were observed for OS (KEAP1WT: R −0.24, P = 0.16; STK11WT: R −0.54, P < 0.01; and KEAP1WT/STK11WT: R −0.47, P = 0.05; Fig. 5F; Supplementary Fig. S6C and S6D). In an exploratory analysis, we found NRF2HIGH status to be associated with significantly worse PFS and OS compared with NRF2LOW status in patients whose tumors are KEAP1WT/STK11WT (Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). In patients whose tumors are KEAP1WT/STK11MUT, we saw a similar trend for worse PFS in patients harboring NRF2HIGH tumors, but not for OS (Supplementary Fig. S7C and S7D). Although limited by the small sample size, these findings suggest that there are factors in STK11MUT tumors that promote resistance to adagrasib beyond KEAP1 co-mutations and NRF2HIGH status. It also suggests that there are KEAP1WT/STK11WT tumors that phenocopy KEAP1MUT tumors and harbor increased NRF2 signaling that ultimately may promote resistance to adagrasib.
Because STK11MUT was associated with shorter PFS and OS to adagrasib monotherapy (Fig. 1), we also investigated whether a STK11/LKB1 signature (16) is associated with clinical outcomes to adagrasib monotherapy. As expected, a high STK11/LKB1 score was enriched in STK11MUT tumors compared with STK11WT tumors (Supplementary Fig. S8A). Although a high STK11/LKB1 score was negatively correlated with PFS upon treatment with adagrasib (R −0.27, P = 0.03), it was not correlated with OS (R −0.18, P = 0.14) or ORR (Supplementary Fig. S8B–S8D). EMT has been previously associated with resistance to targeted therapies (25–28), including KRAS G12Ci (29). However, EMT signature (17) was not correlated with clinical outcomes upon treatment with adagrasib monotherapy in the KRYSTAL-1 trial (Supplementary Fig. S8E–S8G).
KEAP1 and STK11 wild-type and low NRF2 status are collectively associated with improved survival to adagrasib monotherapy
After determining that KEAP1MUT, STK11MUT, and NRF2HIGH transcriptome scores are associated with worse clinical outcomes to adagrasib monotherapy, we hypothesized that the absence of these molecular features would determine a subgroup of patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC with significantly improved clinical outcomes upon treatment with adagrasib.
Fifty patients treated with adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 trial had known mutational status for KEAP1 and STK11 and had transcriptome sequencing data available and were therefore included in this analysis. KEAP1WT/STK11WT/NRF2LOW status was present in 32% (16/50) of patients in this cohort. Patients whose tumor was KEAP1WT/STK11WT/NRF2LOW had significantly longer survival when treated with adagrasib monotherapy compared with those harboring KEAP1MUT, STK11MUT, and/or NRF2HIGH tumors [PFS 12.0 vs. 4.2 months, HR 0.2 (95% CI, 0.1–0.5), log-rank P < 0.01; OS NR vs. 8.0 months, HR 0.1 (95% CI, 0.0–0.5), log-rank P < 0.01; Fig. 6A and B]. The KEAP1WT/STK11WT/NRF2LOW subgroup also had higher 6- and 12-month PFS and OS compared with those whose tumor was KEAP1MUT, STK11MUT, and/or NRF2HIGH (6-month: PFS 91% vs. 28%; OS 100% vs. 56%; 12-month: PFS 42% vs. 5%; OS 83% vs. 31%). Collectively, KEAP1WT, STK11WT, and NRF2LOW status determines a subgroup of patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC with significant and meaningfully longer survival to adagrasib monotherapy.
Discussion
Although KRAS inhibitors are reshaping the therapeutic landscape of KRAS-mutant solid tumors, patients with NSCLC treated with KRAS G12Ci experience nonuniform clinical outcomes ranging from early disease progression to durable clinical benefit (2, 3, 7, 9, 30). Therefore, biomarkers of clinical benefit, or lack thereof, are of paramount importance for the selection of standard-of-care and investigational therapies directed at overcoming or preventing resistance to KRAS G12Ci. Here, we demonstrate that both KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutations are associated with significantly shorter survival upon treatment with the KRAS G12Ci adagrasib. Patients whose tumors were KEAP1WT/STK11WT had significantly longer survival (PFS 16.9 months; OS NR) upon treatment with adagrasib. We demonstrate for the first time that patients whose tumors have increased NRF2 signaling—defined by transcriptome sequencing—also have significantly shorter PFS and OS upon treatment with adagrasib (PFS 4.2 months; OS 6.5 months), and NRF2HIGH score was negatively correlated with PFS and OS even in the absence of KEAP1MUT. We also demonstrate for the first time that when selecting patients based on a KEAP1WT/STK11WT/NRF2LOW status, we distinguish a population—32% of patients—with significant and meaningfully longer PFS (12.0 months, HR 0.2) and OS (NR, HR 0.1) to adagrasib. Collectively, these results further support the use of genomic features—both mutational and nonmutational—for the selection of standard of care and investigational therapies for patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC.
Co-mutations have been previously associated with distinct clinical outcomes to standard therapies such as PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors with or without chemotherapy (13, 31–36) and off-state KRAS G12Ci (9, 10). In the largest cohort to date of KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC (N = 424), we demonstrate that KEAP1MUT were independently associated with shorter PFS and OS to adagrasib and sotorasib monotherapy (9). Similar results were shown in another multi-institutional cohort of patients treated with KRAS G12Ci and in a post hoc analysis of the CodeBreak 100 trial (10, 30). Here, we further validate that KEAP1MUT is associated with worse outcomes to adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 trial, and we provide companion preclinical validation to this clinical finding. In addition, we demonstrate that KEAP1MUT are associated with early disease progression to adagrasib despite ORR of 30% in this subgroup of patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC (Fig. 1E), which suggests that early progression is associated with the emergence of adaptive mechanisms of resistance in these tumors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that one of the main downstream effects of KEAP1 loss—increased NRF2 signaling—is associated with worse clinical outcomes to adagrasib. Although not entirely unexpected, it is clinically relevant that KEAP1WT/NRF2HIGH tumors appear to phenocopy KEAP1MUT tumors and may identify an additional subgroup of patients with early disease progression to adagrasib. These findings highlight a potential nonmutational determinant of clinical outcomes to KRAS G12Ci and corroborate the clinical application of NGS panels that include RNA sequencing for treatment selection and drug discovery in KRAS-mutant NSCLC, which extends beyond mutation profiling. Of note, our findings originate from patients with advanced KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC previously treated with ICI and chemotherapy and might not be generalizable to all stages and disease settings. Future work is required to validate the impact of genomic features on clinical outcomes of KRAS G12Ci in the frontline setting either as a single agent or in combination with ICI. The mechanisms by which KEAP1MUT and increased NRF2 signaling promote resistance to off-state KRAS G12Ci remain undefined. Our group and others have previously reported that STK11MUT and KEAP1MUT are associated with an immune-suppressed tumor microenvironment (37–39). This likely contributes, at least in part, to the poor efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in this genomically defined subgroup of KRAS-mutant NSCLC. It remains unknown if these tumor microenvironment characteristics in the context of STK11MUT and KEAP1MUT also contribute to the impaired efficacy of KRAS G12Ci. Our findings suggest activation of downstream NRF2 target genes converges at least partly on increased activation of the PI3K-mTOR pathway—hereto likely the reason for the increased efficacy of adagrasib and mTOR inhibitor combinations (Fig. 4A and B)—and on reactivation of MAPK signaling by shifting the intracellular pool of RAS to its active GTP-bound state (Supplementary Fig. S2B). Ongoing preclinical work is likely to shed additional light on these mechanisms of early adaptive resistance. The clinical efficacy of novel off-state GDP-RAS [opnurasib (40), olomorasib (41), and divarasib (42)] and on-state GTP-RAS inhibitors [e.g., RMC-6291 (43), RMC-6236 (44, 45), FMC-376 (46), and BBO-8520 (47)] for treatment of co-mutation subtypes of KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC may also provide important insights into these mechanisms of early adaptive resistance.
STK11 MUT were associated with significantly shorter PFS and OS upon treatment with adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 trial (Figs. 1B and D, 2A and B). STK11MUT were previously identified to be enriched in early disease progression to KRAS G12Ci and associated with shorter PFS compared with patients harboring STK11WT tumors upon treatment with KRAS G12Ci (9). However, STK11MUT was not independently associated with poorer survival with sotorasib and adagrasib in the absence of KEAP1MUT in that cohort of patients (9). Additional co-mutations, other than KEAP1, may impact the biology and diminish the therapeutic efficacy of KRAS G12Ci in STK11MUT tumors. One such example would be the SMARCA4 gene, which encodes BRG1, one of two possible and mutually exclusive ATP-dependent core catalytic subunits of mammalian SWI/SNF ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes, and resides near the STK11 gene on the short arm of chromosome 19. The proximity of both genes increases susceptibility to co-deletion events. SMARCA4 mutations have been previously linked with dedifferentiated histology (48), immune checkpoint inhibitor resistance (36, 39), and KRAS G12Ci inhibitor resistance (9). The negative correlation between NRF2 score and survival upon treatment with adagrasib in patients with KEAP1WT tumors (Fig. 5E and F) suggests that selective pressure for increased cellular fitness through increased NRF2 signaling may at least partly explain the worse clinical outcomes to adagrasib in KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC harboring STK11MUT. In fact, 50% of KEAP1WT/STK11MUT tumors in the KRYSTAL-1 trial had an NRF2HIGH score. STK11MUT have also been associated with increased cellular plasticity in KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC, a phenomenon that favors adeno-to-squamous cellular reprogramming and promotes decreased dependency on KRAS signaling and, consequently, adagrasib resistance (15, 49). These data collectively suggest that nongenomic mechanisms may indeed be major drivers of adaptive resistance to KRAS G12Ci in KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC harboring STK11MUT. The sample size of this Krystal-1 cohort limited definitive testing of these hypotheses, but we expect further analyses of clinico-genomic determinants of outcomes to KRAS G12Ci in other larger NSCLC clinical datasets—some of which may also include gene expression data—may be able to more definitively address these questions.
Our preclinical data also shed light on potential combination regimens for treatment intensification to overcome and/or prevent early resistance to adagrasib in KEAP1MUT and STK11MUT NSCLC. Through broad combination drug screens, we demonstrate that adagrasib–mTOR inhibitor combinations provide increased antitumor activity compared with either agent alone, a finding that is aligned with prior reports both for adagrasib and sotorasib (20, 50). We now more clearly define the utility of this combination regimen in the context of STK11MUT and KEAP1MUT. Although we are unable to validate these findings clinically and to assess if NRF2 signaling may clinically impact the efficacy of the KRAS G12Ci and mTOR combination, our findings support further investigation of the KRAS G12Ci and mTOR inhibitor combination for treatment of KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC, particularly as a treatment intensification approach for patients whose tumor harbors STK11MUT and/or KEAP1MUT and for those who develop early disease progression to off-state KRAS G12Ci monotherapy.
In conclusion, KEAP1 and STK11 co-mutations and NRF2 signaling define subgroups of patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC with markedly distinct outcomes upon treatment with adagrasib. KEAP1WT/STK11WT/NRF2LOW status—which accounts for 32% of patients—was associated with significant and meaningfully longer survival to adagrasib. These results further support the use of genomic features—both mutational and nonmutational—for the selection of standard of care and investigational therapies for patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC. Adagrasib combinations with mTOR inhibitors produced higher treatment efficacy compared with adagrasib monotherapy in NSCLC preclinical models, and this combination warrants further investigation for the treatment of patients with KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC whose tumors harbor hard-to-treat co-mutations such as STK11 and/or KEAP1 or that have early disease progression to KRAS G12C off-state inhibitors.
